PROQUEST ECONOMIC DISCOVERY · SECOND SESSION

Other economic outlooks and subsequent employment

A shared economic-outlook signal meets the declared primary multiple-testing screen. Its significance changes with block placement and covariance method, so it remains a candidate finding. Reliable machine-learning forecasting superiority remains unestablished.

What the new association says

The tested gap is employment net direction minus the mean direction of the other supported topics. Conditional on employment direction, its square, neutral share, export coverage and decade effects, a reduction of one standard deviation in that gap corresponds to 0.39 percentage points more unemployment improvement over the following six months (pointwise 95% interval 0.23 to 0.54; pooled Holm p=0.0249). The estimate uses 694 monthly origins and 14 five-year blocks.

For a more natural scale, the same coefficient is 0.25 pp per standard deviation of the other-topic index itself (interval 0.15–0.35). A 0.1-point increase in that index corresponds to 0.12 pp more unemployment improvement. These are equivalent units of the original specified coefficient; its p-value is unchanged.

This is an equivalent parameterization of other-topic information after holding the employment signal fixed. It is not proof that forecasters disagree irrationally about the same proposition. Positive business/market/employment direction means stronger activity, higher stock prices or lower unemployment; positive price direction means rising prices and is not called good news.

Controlling earlier survey measures of consumers’ current and expected conditions retains an association of 0.24 pp per original other-topic-index SD (pooled Holm p=0.0493; 607 origins). This is a second test of the same substantive lead, not a second independent economic discovery. The survey download is a retrospective reconstruction covariate; its exact historical vintages and release dates are not claimed as model inputs.

Shared information is the clearest interpretation

A PCA component learned only from earlier business, market and price outlooks is associated with 0.34 pp subsequent unemployment improvement per SD (interval 0.21–0.47; pooled Holm p=0.0249; 658 origins). It enters jointly with an employment-specific residual, so total employment outlook can change with the common component. The separate employment-residual coefficient does not clear the full testing correction; that does not prove its contribution is zero.

The other-topic mean also remains associated after two disjoint article halves of employment outlooks enter the regression (pooled Holm p=0.0493). These are related measurements of the same historical pattern, not independent discoveries or new holdouts.

A second indicator can improve inference about a persistent current state without containing uniquely forward-looking content. The hypothetical model below demonstrates that interpretation; its parameters are illustrative and were not estimated from this archive. The actual data do not identify which mechanism dominates.

How far the evidence goes

The point estimate persists in raw exports, publisher omissions, a two-paper coverage restriction, year effects and earlier print cutoffs. Fresh macro controls reduce it; controlling broad newspaper tone and macro data together leaves an interval spanning zero. Ten-year exact inference has very few clusters and does not support family-wide rejection. The primary five-year finding is therefore conditional on its dependence assumptions and machine interpretation.

Block placement changes the strength of inference

All five placements of five-year calendar blocks were retained. The simple gap fails the full-search threshold for several placements. The shared PCA coefficient passes the primary cluster/wild test at every placement, but fails some jackknife variants. No coefficient is uniformly significant across every reasonable dependence specification, and no favorable anchor replaces the original. This is a material qualification of the primary result.

The fitted point coefficients stay unchanged when the block anchor moves. What changes is the grouping of regression scores: positive and negative annual contributions cancel differently within blocks, changing the estimated uncertainty. This is a covariance sensitivity, not a different economic point estimate.

Measurement challenges

The point estimate persists when only stated horizons supply the signal and when employment and other-topic directions come from the same articles. These narrower samples do not retain the full family-wide rejection. Requiring all four topics in each article leaves only 107 supported origins and an interval spanning zero. These restrictions address composition; machine-stated horizons and directions still need source verification.

Calibration limits

Forty thousand fixed-design simulations combine six-month overlapping errors with four specified innovation autocorrelations. At a nominal 5% level, the primary cluster/wild maximum rejects approximately 5.5–7.4% of true nulls in these illustrative cases. The block jackknife rejects approximately 1.4–4.3%. Thus exact enumeration of bootstrap signs is not an exact finite-sample guarantee about the null distribution. That pilot alone samples the extreme family-level tail too sparsely to assess its calibration precisely; the larger runs below address that numerical limitation. These simulations neither validate source labels nor establish that the real errors follow any of the simulated processes.

Controls compared on identical origins and effect units

On the same 521 origins, adding the historical macro controls changes the other-topic point coefficient from about 0.245 to 0.175 pp per original other-index SD. On the same 368 tone-supported origins, the base estimate is about 0.323 and the tone-plus-macro estimate is about 0.211. Thus control attenuation is not solely a change in sample or standard-deviation units. The shorter samples also have fewer calendar blocks, limiting the attainable adjusted significance.

What the unemployment association represents

A descriptive accounting check uses the same 694 origins. The implied unemployment-improvement coefficient is approximately 0.247 pp, with a 0.275 pp employment-level contribution and a −0.028 pp labor-force contribution. The point pattern therefore aligns with employment gains rather than primarily with labor-force contraction. Payroll and household employment growth also have positive point coefficients. These are accounting and benchmark diagnostics without a new significance test or an identified causal mechanism.

Machine learning: gains, uncertainty and the benchmark

Four model families—linear regression/logistic regression, histogram gradient boosting, extra trees and a small unidirectional GRU—use 408 common monthly origins in 1977–2010. Every January, model settings are selected using earlier chronological folds and historical-vintage labels. Every arm shares macro inputs and export-coverage controls. Adding four topic nets and then 32 structural features supplies the two specified comparisons. The GRU uses structured monthly label histories; no raw article text is locally available to this experiment.

For unemployment, the linear macro-plus-coverage baseline has MSE 0.307, versus 0.375 for boosted trees. Adding topic nets improves the boosted-tree point estimate to 0.299. That is a substantial within-model improvement, but it also shows why gains against a weaker nonlinear baseline do not establish superiority to a stronger forecasting process.

None of these primary model additions survives the full correction. The joint block-multiplier diagnostics below repeat inner selection for the linear procedure; nonlinear diagnostics hold the originally selected settings fixed. They recompute weighted preprocessing and every chronological fit, averaging all three declared neural seeds. Multiplier ranges are sensitivity diagnostics, not a replacement significant p-value or a correction for semantic label error.

Power and test resolution. The 34-year ML evaluation has seven five-year blocks. An enumerated two-sided sign test has a minimum attainable p of 2/2⁷ = 0.015625, which cannot cross the pooled 204-question threshold. Even two-year-block sensitivities do not produce a corrected model gain. The primary failure to reject therefore does not establish equivalence or zero information. More simulations or a larger neural network cannot create additional historical evaluation blocks.

Stronger benchmark combinations

Two descriptive combination rules were constructed after inspecting the original results: equal-weight forecasts from all four families, and selection of the family with the lowest earlier inner-validation loss at each yearly refit. Choices and forecasts were saved before attaching evaluation truth. The equal ensemble improves some point losses with topic signals; prior-validation family selection gives no continuous-unemployment improvement. These adaptive diagnostics receive no new p-value or independent discovery claim.

All three neural initializations retained

Reconstructing every declared seed reproduces the original average within numerical precision. For production growth, structural features raise the loss of each individual seed, yet reduce ensemble MSE by about 0.083. The exact squared-loss decomposition attributes that small gain to the larger benefit from averaging dispersed predictions: mean individual-seed loss rises by about 0.533, while the averaging benefit rises by about 0.616. This is a property of these three fitted seeds, with no new test or evidence about independent economic cycles.

For production growth, its MSE is about 7.408; the GRU with topic nets has MSE about 7.368, an almost negligible point gain compared with the much larger gain against the GRU’s own weaker baseline. Other questions were retained, including the nulls

  • Confidence/voice differences, horizon structure, revision, breadth and variance components mostly fail the adjusted screen.
  • Real-activity/price expectation combinations and same-article co-movement do not establish a corrected discovery.
  • Industry employment outlooks show a positive nominal association, but none of the six industry/regional/foreign indicator tests survives correction. They are indicator tests, not individual forecast accuracy against national outcomes.
  • The cross-topic future-versus-recent timing contrast is nominally positive in the other-topic parameterization but fails the full screen; it does not independently establish foresight.
  • A new six-month stock-price-decline task uses 972 origins in 1930–2010. Its target and -10 log-percent threshold are fixed. The Shiller price history is a retrospective broad-market proxy; this is not an executable trading strategy or exact historical index-vintage test.

The market task uses only price history, never interpolated dividends, earnings or valuation ratios. Nevertheless, its long price series is a retrospective reconstruction with weaker real-time provenance than the native-vintage macro models. Treat it as a reconstruction diagnostic; its lag checks alone do not establish exact historical index availability.

The previous confidence contrast, which passed the 68-test screen, no longer clears pooled Holm after this expanded search. Its source-measurement qualification also remains. Rows describing the same substantive signal are not counted as multiple independent economic discoveries.

Scope, timing and what significance does not validate

Only the 111 annual verified ProQuest exports, 1900–2010, supply primary claims. The matching 111 annual raw exports supply sensitivity data. There are no pooled LOC claims, old crisis-window exports, or modern claims. Identical stripped labels remain; article averaging is weighting, not deduplication. All 222 annual source hashes remain unchanged.

Features are explicitly whitelisted printed metadata. No retrospective window annotations, verifier prose, economic outcomes, or outcome eligibility enter them. Monthly signals use completed earlier print months. Macro forecasts use native historical production vintages and exact prior-as-of unemployment snapshots, with endpoint+three months strictly before each fitting or selection cutoff. Missing source coverage is missing, not neutral sentiment. Export counts do not measure population newspaper attention.

Claims remain machine interpreted. The existing historical human sample is too small to reconstruct a validated monthly panel or establish the confidence advantage. Strong temporal p-values cannot repair a false forecast, wrong topic, wrong scope or wrong horizon. Current results establish conditional relationships in the selected archive; they establish neither causation nor distinct information beyond every existing predictor.

An outcome-blind probability sample is prepared for source review of the employment lead: 14 calendar-stratified origins, 4189 articles and 9932 machine panel rows. The reviewer file withholds machine labels and outcomes. Original article text is not locally available, so this is a prepared packet, not completed human validation. Its frame excludes articles without readable machine panel labels and therefore cannot estimate newspaper-wide recall.

Novelty. Published work already uses newspaper sentiment, topics and common factors to model output and employment. The candidate contribution here is a specific cross-topic contrast in this historical forecast-claim archive. The present evidence does not establish a first-in-literature finding or prove that its information is distinct from the current economic state and broader news tone.

Historical length alone is also insufficient: Bybee and coauthors extend topic attention back to 1890, while van Binsbergen and coauthors study roughly 170 years of local-newspaper sentiment. The comparison table records the narrower measurement distinction and the evidence still missing. The forecasting exercises here use different data and targets from those papers and are not direct replications.

Cross-variable forecast consistency also has an established literature, including aligned output and unemployment forecasts and recent WEO-coherence research. Directions taken from different articles, targets and horizons do not supply the matched quantitative objects needed to infer individual incoherence or an Okun-law violation.

Primary literature and external benchmarks

  • (Almost) 200 Years of News-Based Economic Sentiment: Long historical newspaper sentiment already predicts activity; generic newspaper predictability is not a novelty claim. Investigate public aggregate data as an external retrospective tone control, not a source of pooled claims.
  • The Term Structure of Expectations: Professional forecast horizons and joint-variable expectation dynamics have precedents. Our sparse stated-horizon groups do not establish a term-structure contribution.
  • Overreaction in Macroeconomic Expectations: Forecast revision/error tests require aligned forecasts. A directional aggregate revision coefficient alone does not establish overreaction.
  • Manufacturing Sentiment: Forecasting Industrial Production with Text Analysis: Demonstrates text models with direct human and naturally occurring labels. Our structured-label GRU has no local raw text and needs independent semantic validation.
  • Forecasting U.S. Economic Activity with a Small Information Set: Motivates stronger labor/sentiment/interest/credit benchmarks; exact monthly historical financial vintages are not available in ALFRED before1996 for the inspected series.
  • Measuring economic outlook in the news: Further precedent for modern text-based GDP forecast improvements; a successful RNN by itself is not a distinctive economic contribution.
  • Prediction-Powered Inference: Human-assisted inference is relevant, but a sparse claim sample cannot nonparametrically reconstruct every monthly topic signal. Repeated model self-review is not independent human validation.
  • National Archives: Electoral College and election calendar: The election-window feature uses the known historical presidential-election schedule. Attribution labels do not establish party or incumbent identity.
  • Electoral Cycles in Macroeconomic Forecasts: Prior research directly studies government forecast optimism in campaigns. The current coarse voice-label tests do not establish the corresponding effect.
  • BLS nonfarm-business labor productivity via FRED: Revised outcome benchmark only; six-month two-quarter growth, no causal technology-shock interpretation.
  • BLS real hourly compensation via FRED: Average real compensation per hour, not median worker pay or a direct inequality measure.
  • BLS labor-share index via FRED: Changes are in a rebased index, not percentage-point changes in the literal labor share.
  • Business News and Business Cycles (Bybee, Kelly, Manela and Xiu; NBER29344, published Journal of Finance2024): Topic-based business-news information already models macroeconomic dynamics. Our cross-topic coefficient is not evidence that news as a forecasting input is a new idea.
  • Making text count: economic forecasting using newspaper text (Bank of England working paper865): Primary supervised-text forecasting comparison for GDP, inflation and unemployment; useful context for why ML architecture alone is not an economic contribution.
  • Bad News, Good News: Coverage and Response Asymmetries (Norges Bank working paper8/2022): Economic-news asymmetry can reflect asymmetric underlying unemployment dynamics. Supports careful separation of coverage, expectations and economic state.
  • Nowcasting GDP using tone-adjusted time varying news topics (De Nederlandsche Bank working paper766): An existing topic/factor approach to macro nowcasting; PCA/shared-source information is not automatically novel.
  • US monthly economic policy uncertainty: provider methodology: Historical reconstruction and changing newspaper sets overlap the ProQuest archive. Used only as an historical conditioning descriptor, never a real-time ML feature.
  • BLS establishment payroll employment: Current revised historical levels are used only for descriptive outcome/accounting interpretation, never as historical ML inputs.
  • BLS household employment level: Current revised historical levels are used only for descriptive outcome/accounting interpretation, never as historical ML inputs.
  • BLS civilian labor-force level: Current revised historical levels are used only for descriptive outcome/accounting interpretation, never as historical ML inputs.
  • Do Forecasters Believe in Okun’s Law? An Assessment of Unemployment and Output Forecasts (IMF WP14/24): Joint unemployment/output forecast consistency has an established literature using aligned quantitative Consensus forecasts. Our multi-topic directional gap, pooled across articles and horizons, is not an Okun-law or individual-rationality test.
  • Looking for Underlying Structure in WEO Forecasts (IMF WP2026/164): Recent primary work already studies forecast comovement and growth/inflation coherence. We do not pool WEO observations or claim our heterogeneous newspaper directions replicate its aligned projections.

Reproduce and inspect

Use the working scientific Python environment for panels and regression; the isolated /private/tmp/proquest-ml-20261023/bin/python contains the model libraries. Do not use the broken repository-root environment. All source data and previous results remain unchanged. The final manifest records code, input, environment and output hashes. Work on a copy for regeneration: rebuilding updates derived files covered by that manifest.

The environment freezes are saved under audits/; the temporary ML environment may need to be recreated later. Full analysis entry points and their specifications are retained in this directory. For additional replications, copy the result directory and use the explicit-deadline wrapper, which checks frozen model dependencies and library versions before fitting. The original sampler CLI preserves the session’s fixed stop time, so it should not be used directly to resume after that date. Initial model outputs remain for the numerical audit.
